observations: A face fills the upper two-thirds: olive-yellow skin tones with deep black voids where eyes would be, long dark hair falling straight on both sides against a muted grey-green ground.
Dense white scribble lines layer across the face—looping, crossing, clustering near the forehead and cheeks—sitting visibly above the tonal underlayer rather than blending into it.
The lower quarter is dominated by a flat black shape crossed by a white geometric net of irregular polygons with solid white dots at each node, cutting hard against the softer face above.
reading: The black eye sockets read as absence rather than gaze, and the white scribble lines feel like static laid over a face already receding into olive-grey tones. The net at the bottom—rigid, diagrammatic—presses against that softness like a different system entirely. The collision between the two is where the image holds tension.
contextAngle: Within the owned nifty-faces subset, this work sits between title neighbors #68 and #70. Where #68 rings a vivid teal face with yellow dots and wide white eyes, and #70 blazes in orange with dense color blocks, #69 pulls toward near-monochrome restraint.

connections.reason: Both works use solid white dots at net or border nodes, but #68 rings them around a saturated face while #69 anchors them in a flat black band beneath a drained one—same device, opposite color temperature.
rawblocks #54 shares the olive-yellow skin tone and black-void eye treatment, and pale incised lines over dark ground describe the face in both—the visible quality the collector links to scrimshaw.

lookingQuestion: Where exactly does the white net end and the white scribble lines begin—and does the boundary between them hold or dissolve?
ambiguities: The white lines on the face could be a separate layer or part of the same mark-making pass as the net; the image alone cannot confirm layer order.
The rawblocks #54 comparison is cross-collection; the formal resemblance is visible but whether it reflects a shared approach cannot be determined from images alone.
